# Improving UAV Attitude Control with Cascaded PID: Methods, Evidence, and Optimal Parameter Selection

A fixed cascaded PID controller is a strong baseline for UAV attitude control, but one gain set is normally a local solution: it is tuned for a particular vehicle, payload, thrust level, speed, delay, and disturbance environment. PX4 and ArduPilot both document a cascade in which an outer attitude loop generates angular-rate commands and an inner rate PID drives the actuators; this architecture is widely used, although the available evidence does not establish a complete census proving that most open-source flight controllers use it. The most reliable improvements are therefore layered: calibrate the plant, tune the inner rate loop before the outer attitude loop, add filtering, feedforward, anti-windup, saturation handling, and disturbance compensation, then use gain scheduling or bounded adaptation when operating conditions genuinely change. Optimal parameters are not universal constants; they are the solution of a constrained, mission-specific trade-off among tracking error, transient response, control effort, robustness, actuator limits, noise, computation, and safety.

This report first explains why fixed gains lose performance across the flight envelope. It then compares state-dependent scheduling, adaptive and intelligent PID methods, and practical enhancements that preserve the PID structure. The final sections describe how to select gains for cascaded loops, compare evidence from simulation, hardware-in-the-loop and flight experiments, and give recommendations for open-source flight-controller development.

## 1. The cascaded PID baseline and the varying-flight-state problem

### 1.1 What the open-source baseline actually contains

A cascaded controller separates a fast inner loop from a slower outer loop. For attitude control, the outer loop compares desired and measured attitude and converts the attitude error into a desired body angular rate. The inner loop compares that rate command with the measured gyro rate and produces torque or actuator commands.

PX4 describes its multicopter controller as a standard cascaded architecture containing a mixture of proportional and PID controllers. The angular-rate controller is the innermost loop and uses independent PID controllers for roll, pitch, and yaw; the attitude controller supplies the rate setpoints. PX4 also documents integral limits, actuator-output limits, derivative filtering, reference-model smoothing, rate feedforward, and mixer saturation handling as part of the practical implementation ([PX4 multicopter controller and tuning guide](https://docs.px4.io/main/en/flight_stack/controller_diagrams), [PX4 multicopter PID tuning guide](https://docs.px4.io/main/en/config_mc/pid_tuning_guide_multicopter)).

ArduPilot documents a similar two-layer attitude path. An angle-P controller converts angle error into desired angular velocity, and a rate PID controller converts rate error into the final motor command. On the documented hardware paths, the update loop runs at 400 Hz on Pixhawk and 100 Hz on APM2.x before commands reach the motor mixer ([ArduPilot attitude-control implementation](https://ardupilot.org/dev/docs/apmcopter-programming-attitude-control-2.html), [ArduPilot attitude architecture](https://deepwiki.com/ArduPilot/ardupilot/2.3-attitude-and-position-control)).

| Controller or source | Cascaded structure | Practical implementation features |
|---|---|---|
| PX4 multicopter | Attitude P/reference model → body-rate PID → mixer | Integral limiting, derivative low-pass filtering, rate limits, reference-rate feedforward, actuator and mixer saturation handling |
| ArduPilot Copter | Angle P → rate PID → motor mixing | Bounded integrator, body-rate feedforward, throttle–attitude mixing, vehicle-specific subclasses and command-slew limits |
| Betaflight | Rate-control PID with state-dependent scheduler | Gain scheduling by throttle and battery-voltage levels is documented in the literature |
| General quadrotor designs | Outer position or attitude loop → inner attitude or rate loop | Loop frequencies, gains, filters, and actuator limits are selected according to the vehicle and mission |

The wider literature also describes PID as the predominant or most commonly used controller for UAV and quadrotor flight control. Surveys attribute that position to PID’s simple structure, low computational cost, intuitive terms, and acceptable nominal performance ([ACM quadrotor-control survey](https://doi.org/10.1145/3617652), [UAV autopilot and reinforcement-learning study](https://cs-web.bu.edu/faculty/richwest/papers/tcps2019.pdf)). PX4 explicitly presents itself as an open-source autopilot for drone developers and is used in research, consumer-drone, and industrial applications ([PX4 project](https://px4.io/)).

That evidence supports the practical baseline, but it does not establish a current, comprehensive inventory or percentage for the entire open-source flight-controller ecosystem. The strongest defensible statement is that PX4 and ArduPilot, together with other widely used firmware such as Betaflight, provide prominent examples of cascaded or PID-based open-source flight control. A universal prevalence percentage is unavailable.

### 1.2 Why a locally tuned gain set is only locally optimal

For a single body axis, a simplified rotational model near hover can be written as

$$J_i\dot{\omega}_i \approx \tau_i+d_i,$$

where \(J_i\) is the moment of inertia, \(\omega_i\) is angular rate, \(\tau_i\) is commanded control torque, and \(d_i\) represents disturbances and unmodelled effects. If the inertia changes while the controller is unchanged, the same torque produces a different angular acceleration. The effective plant seen by the PID therefore changes even if the software and nominal gains remain identical.

The principal sources of variation are the following.

#### Payload and inertia

Adding a payload changes total mass, center of gravity, and often the roll, pitch, and yaw inertias. A payload mounted away from the center can increase one rotational inertia much more than another. A gain set that produces a well-damped rate response on an empty vehicle may become sluggish after loading, while an aggressive set may become oscillatory if a different payload changes the motor authority or coupling.

A 2022 control study describes payload uncertainty as a direct reason for fixed-gain degradation: when total mass changes, gains designed for one configuration no longer match the plant. Its actor–critic adaptive PID reduced simulated attitude RMSE under mass uncertainty and wind, but the evidence was simulation-based rather than a physical flight test ([online actor–critic PID study](https://arxiv.org/html/2307.01312v1)). A real-flight study by Diaz Luengo, Bordeneuve-Guibé, and Defay tested a quadcopter that dropped at least 30% of its nominal weight. The study compared gain scheduling with model-reference adaptive control and found that both limited the altitude excursion after the drop, while MRAC recovered the original altitude in 6 s and gain scheduling in 9 s during the reported mission ([variable-payload MRAC and gain-scheduling study](https://www.imavs.org/papers/2019/21.pdf)).

These results concern a position and altitude cascade rather than an isolated inner attitude step response, so they should be interpreted as evidence for the payload-adaptation mechanism, not as a universal ranking of attitude controllers.

#### Speed and aerodynamic effects

Aerodynamic drag and control effectiveness vary with airspeed. For a fixed-wing aircraft, PX4 warns that gains tuned tightly at cruise speed can produce oscillation at higher airspeed or poor tracking at lower airspeed if airspeed scaling is absent. Its documented compensation scales rate-PI output with indicated airspeed squared and rate feedforward with true airspeed, reflecting changes in dynamic pressure and aerodynamic damping. For an aircraft operating from 15 to 25 m/s, PX4 recommends tuning near 20 m/s and emphasizes that airspeed-sensor quality directly affects performance ([PX4 controller diagrams and airspeed scaling](https://docs.px4.io/main/en/flight_stack/controller_diagrams)).

For multirotors, high translational speed changes drag and can intensify inertial coupling and attitude demand. A 2026 LPV study models drag as proportional to velocity squared and uses forward velocity as a scheduling variable, with local models at 0, 5, 10, and 15 m/s ([hierarchical safety-constrained adaptive PID study](https://doi.org/10.3390/aerospace13050446)). The numerical grid is not a universal prescription; it is a vehicle-specific approximation of one flight envelope.

#### Thrust level, battery voltage, and actuator nonlinearity

Multicopter gains are often tuned around hover thrust. At higher throttle, motor and propeller dynamics, thrust linearity, ESC behavior, and available torque can differ substantially. PX4 therefore provides a thrust-model factor, `THR_MDL_FAC`, that interpolates between a linear and quadratic PWM-to-thrust mapping. Typical values are reported as 0.3–0.5, but PX4 recommends measuring thrust against motor command where possible because static thrust depends strongly on battery voltage. Changing the thrust model may require rate-loop retuning ([PX4 multicopter tuning guide](https://docs.px4.io/main/en/config_mc/pid_tuning_guide_multicopter)).

A gain set that works at a charged battery can therefore produce different closed-loop behavior as voltage falls. The controller is not simply controlling an abstract torque; it is controlling a motor command passed through a voltage-dependent, nonlinear actuator.

#### Wind, drag torque, and unmodelled disturbances

Wind can create translational forces and rotational moments. The integral term can remove a persistent rate or attitude offset, but it is a reactive mechanism: it must first accumulate error. Sudden gusts, changing drag, and coupling can exceed the available actuator authority before the integral term has time to respond. The PX4 architecture discussion describes the rate-loop integrator as primarily useful for rejecting persistent effects such as air drag and wind ([PX4 cascaded-control architecture discussion](https://discuss.px4.io/t/multicopter-control-architecture-design-choices/31815)).

A 2022 Sensors study similarly reports that fixed-frequency PID control generalizes poorly across trajectories and changing external disturbances. Its contribution schedules the relative frequencies of the attitude and position loops rather than directly scheduling gains, but the underlying observation is relevant: the best closed-loop configuration depends on the operating task and disturbance ([frequency-scheduled PID study](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8220/22/1/150)).

#### Coupling, large attitudes, and aggressive manoeuvres

The quadrotor is underactuated: four principal control inputs influence six degrees of freedom. At small angles and low rates, roll, pitch, and yaw channels can often be approximated as weakly coupled. During aggressive manoeuvres, the gyroscopic terms, motor dynamics, aerodynamic drag, attitude transformation, and mixer interaction become more important. A PID tuned from a hover-local linearization may not preserve the same phase margin or damping away from hover.

Bolandi et al. explicitly linearize the quadrotor model around hovering and omit gyroscopic effects in the controller design. Their approach is useful for a local analytical design, but the stated assumptions define its operating boundary ([Bolandi et al. optimized PID study](https://file.scirp.org/Html/12-7900231_35654.htm)). Similarly, a 2023 comparative study designs inner-loop PID controllers around the hover equilibrium and evaluates them in a nonlinear simulation; the result demonstrates a hover-based design, not a guarantee across the complete envelope ([Rinaldi, Primatesta, and Guglieri](https://doi.org/10.3390/app13063464)).

#### Sensor noise, filtering, and delay

The derivative term responds to high-frequency measurement noise. Excessive derivative gain can produce motor twitching and heating, while excessive filtering introduces phase lag. Sensor and communication delays reduce the phase margin available to the rate loop. A design that is stable with ideal measurements may become unstable when IMU filtering, estimator delay, wireless communication, actuator response, and mixer computation are included.

The problem is visible in experimental neural and fuzzy studies. The Tello fuzzy-neural study attributes part of the limited physical advantage over simulation to wireless UDP delay and to the mapping from force and torque commands into the drone’s four remote-control channels ([cascade fuzzy-neural PID study](https://doi.org/10.3390/en15051763)). The same issue exists in a conventional PID implementation; an intelligent algorithm cannot recover phase margin that has been consumed by unmodelled delay.

### 1.3 Fixed PID is not the same as a bare, unprotected PID

The statement that fixed PID is “poorly robust” usually refers to a bare, locally tuned controller evaluated under substantial parameter variation or disturbance. A practical flight stack often adds integral limits, derivative filters, feedforward, mixer logic, reference shaping, actuator saturation handling, and estimator filtering. Those additions can make a fixed-gain controller effective over a useful operating envelope even though the gains themselves do not change.

This distinction explains an apparent disagreement in the literature. One source describes PID as unable to handle constraints and poorly robust to disturbances and uncertainty ([Rinaldi et al.](https://doi.org/10.3390/app13063464)). Open-source implementations nevertheless address constraints through saturation limits, anti-windup, mixer allocation, slew limits, and bounded setpoints. The correct conclusion is not that one source is wrong: bare PID does not enforce all physical constraints by itself, while a safeguarded PID stack can.

## 2. Gain scheduling and state-dependent PID methods

### 2.1 What gain scheduling changes

Gain scheduling keeps the PID structure but makes its parameters functions of a measured or estimated scheduling variable \(s\):

$$K_p=K_p(s),\qquad K_i=K_i(s),\qquad K_d=K_d(s).$$

The scheduler may select a complete controller from a finite table, interpolate between controllers, scale the control output, or interpolate a family of local models and associated gains. The important requirement is that the scheduling variable correlates with a change in the plant and is available reliably enough for real-time use.

Common scheduling variables include:

- airspeed or forward velocity;
- throttle or estimated thrust;
- battery voltage;
- payload mass or estimated total mass;
- estimated inertia or center-of-gravity condition;
- attitude angle, angular rate, or manoeuvre class;
- flight mode or transition state;
- aerodynamic or actuator operating point.

The scheduling variable can be exogenous, such as measured airspeed, or endogenous, such as tracking error, attitude, or motor command. Endogenous scheduling is more responsive but creates another feedback path that must be bounded and filtered.

### 2.2 Lookup-table and operating-point schedules

#### Airspeed and actuator scaling

PX4’s fixed-wing airspeed scaling is a simple but important form of state-dependent control. It does not necessarily replace one PID table with another. Instead, it scales the rate-PI and feedforward contributions according to airspeed so that the controller’s authority tracks aerodynamic effectiveness. This is attractive when the relevant physical relationship is known and the sensor is trustworthy.

Betaflight provides a multirotor example of direct gain scheduling: the firmware is described as adjusting PID gains according to throttle and voltage levels ([Koch et al.](https://cs-web.bu.edu/faculty/richwest/papers/tcps2019.pdf)). The available evidence establishes the implementation, but not a standardized quantitative comparison of tracking error, settling time, or disturbance rejection against a fixed Betaflight tune.

#### Families of locally tuned controllers

Poksawat, Wang, and Mohamed developed an automatically tuned family of cascaded PID controllers for a fixed-wing UAV at several airspeed operating points. An airspeed sensor selected the operating condition, and interpolation between linear closed-loop family members was used to provide a smooth transition. Wind-tunnel experiments reported improvement over a nonadaptive linear controller ([Poksawat, Wang, and Mohamed](https://doi.org/10.1109/tcst.2017.2709274)).

The general construction procedure is:

1. Define the operating envelope and select scheduling variables.
2. Identify or linearize the plant at representative operating points.
3. Tune a PID controller at each point, preferably with common performance and robustness specifications.
4. Validate each local controller and the interpolated controllers.
5. Interpolate gains or closed-loop parameters during operation.
6. Add rate limits, hysteresis, and fallback logic to prevent rapid switching.

A table indexed by one variable is easy to implement. A multidimensional table indexed by speed, payload, voltage, and attitude can become large and sparse. Interpolation can reduce the number of stored points, but it does not automatically preserve stability between them. Stability must be checked over the interpolation region or protected by conservative bounds.

#### Payload and mass scheduling

Payload scheduling is useful when the dominant variation is repeatable and measurable. Diaz Luengo et al. used mass and inertia as scheduling variables and optimized gain tables for loaded and unloaded configurations. Their online mass estimate used vertical velocity and throttle. A naive estimate was reactive but error-prone; recursive least squares with forgetting factor \(\lambda=0.98\) was slower but more stable. The authors combined fast detection of a payload drop with estimation and error checking ([variable-payload MRAC and gain-scheduling study](https://www.imavs.org/papers/2019/21.pdf)).

The flight experiment illustrates both the value and the limit of scheduling. With a 400 g additional mass dropped after approximately 60 s of a 120 s mission, both gain scheduling and MRAC limited post-drop altitude gain to no more than 30 cm. Gain scheduling returned to the original altitude in 9 s, while MRAC did so in 6 s. The authors judged MRAC better over the full mission but found gain scheduling more reactive during the loaded segment. In another experiment, MRAC adapted successfully between a 1.360 kg Mikrokopter Mk.6 and a 0.713 kg Parrot AR using the same controller structure and initial gains, whereas gain scheduling required accurate mass and payload information.

This is a useful counterexample to the claim that one method is always superior. Gain scheduling can be faster when the operating state is known and switching is immediate. Model-reference adaptation can cover conditions that were not included in the table, but its adaptation gains require careful selection and its transient response can be slower or more variable.

#### Multi-model and LPV scheduling

A more systematic form of scheduling uses a linear parameter-varying (LPV) model. The nonlinear plant is represented as an interpolation of local linear models:

$$A(\rho)=\sum_{k=1}^{N}\mu_k(\rho)A_k,\qquad B(\rho)=\sum_{k=1}^{N}\mu_k(\rho)B_k,\qquad \mu_k\geq0,\quad\sum_k\mu_k=1.$$

Here \(\rho\) is the scheduling parameter and \(\mu_k\) are interpolation weights. Local PID gains can be selected for each model, or the PID can be written as structured state feedback and designed with common stability constraints.

The 2020 IEEE Access study combines real-time identification, operating-mode discretization, and phase-margin constraints. It identifies local descriptions for conditions such as near-ground hover and large translational speed. Its model grid is selected according to deterioration of controller performance; the study uses integral squared error and a 10% adjacent-process cost as a discretization criterion, while noting that constructing the grid can take days or weeks depending on the selected parameter range ([real-time multirotor identification and scheduling study](https://doi.org/10.1109/access.2020.3006277)).

Kazemi and Tarighi retain a PID-based structure while using a polytopic LPV model, principal-component mapping of parameter sets, robust pole assignment, and LMI-based \(H_\infty\) disturbance attenuation. The design guarantees an attenuation level for tracking error under wind disturbance in simulation, but the supplied evidence does not include hardware-in-the-loop or flight validation ([Kazemi and Tarighi](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40435-023-01372-6)).

The 2026 safety-constrained RL-PID study uses a related hierarchy. It fixes inner attitude and rate gains using LPV/LMI conditions at four velocity vertices, then adapts outer-loop gains inside an LMI-derived safe domain. The theoretical guarantee applies to the fixed inner parameters at the selected vertices; the online outer-loop policy is protected by gain bounds and Lagrangian penalties, which the authors correctly describe as an engineering safeguard rather than a global stability proof ([Tian et al.](https://doi.org/10.3390/aerospace13050446)).

### 2.3 Transition handling is part of the controller

A table of gains is not complete without a transition policy. Poor transitions can negate the benefit of scheduling.

The principal transition mechanisms are:

- continuous interpolation between neighboring gain sets;
- hysteresis around switching thresholds;
- minimum dwell time;
- bounded gain slew rate;
- filtered scheduling variables;
- bumpless transfer of integrator states;
- saturation-aware switching;
- fallback to a validated baseline when the scheduler signal is invalid.

Poksawat et al. explicitly use interpolation to make transitions smooth. The Concordia fault-tolerance study uses a linear transition between gain modes and reports that gain scheduling reacts faster than MRAC only when the switching time is kept close to zero. That result makes the transition requirement explicit: the benefit depends not only on the gain values but also on how quickly and smoothly they are applied ([Concordia gain-scheduled PID and MRAC experiment](https://doi.org/10.21535/dj2zd771)).

A practical implementation should also decide what happens to the integral state. If \(K_i\) changes while the integrator is retained unchanged, the integral contribution can jump. Possible remedies are to preserve the actual integral contribution, rescale the stored state when the gain changes, or freeze adaptation while the actuator is saturated. The exact transformation depends on the PID form, so it should be verified against the implementation rather than copied as a universal formula.

### 2.4 Advantages and limits

Gain scheduling is usually the most transparent way to extend a fixed PID controller:

- It preserves the familiar control law and failure modes.
- It adds little runtime computation.
- Its behavior can be inspected in a table or scaling equation.
- Each operating point can be validated independently.
- It can use model-based or empirical gains.

Its limitations are equally important:

- The relevant scheduling variable must be measurable or estimable.
- The table must cover the actual envelope.
- Multiple simultaneous changes can require a high-dimensional table.
- An erroneous estimate can select unsafe gains.
- Interpolation may not preserve stability automatically.
- The controller may remain poor between operating points if the plant changes in an unmodelled way.

For a known, repeatable operating variation such as airspeed, throttle, battery voltage, or payload class, scheduling is often preferable to unrestricted online learning.

## 3. Adaptive, self-tuning, and intelligent PID methods

### 3.1 Adaptive control, self-tuning, and intelligent PID are different

These terms are often used interchangeably, but they describe different mechanisms.

- **Self-tuning or autotuning** identifies the plant or observes a response and computes new PID gains, usually during a dedicated procedure.
- **Adaptive PID** updates parameters during ordinary operation according to an adaptation law, a model-reference error, an online estimator, or a recursive identification method.
- **Fuzzy PID** uses linguistic rules and membership functions to map error, error rate, or other variables to gains or gain increments.
- **Neural PID** learns a nonlinear mapping from measured states or errors to gains, compensation terms, or control commands.
- **Reinforcement-learning PID** trains a policy to choose gains or gain increments according to a reward and safety constraints.
- **Iterative learning control** uses error from repeated trajectories or missions to improve future feedforward or PID-related parameters.

The historical progression is from manual and classical tuning, through frequency-response and relay-based autotuning, to gain scheduling, model-reference adaptation, fuzzy rules, neural approximators, and reinforcement learning. Each step increases potential envelope coverage but also adds assumptions, parameters, computation, validation burden, and safety concerns.

### 3.2 Self-tuning and autotuning

#### PX4 autotune

PX4 autotune injects small disturbances into each axis and uses system identification to calculate rate or attitude parameters. The procedure takes approximately 40 s, with a documented range of 19–70 s. Its identification model assumes a linear, uncoupled SISO system with two poles and two zeros. PX4 states that the procedure generally works for supported multicopter and fixed-wing configurations when the frame is not too flexible, but warns that noise, vibration, delay, saturation, slew-rate limits, and airframe flexibility can degrade identification ([PX4 autotune documentation](https://github.com/PX4/PX4-Autopilot/blob/c76c8f55/docs/en/config/_autotune.md)).

The safety logic is significant:

- The vehicle must already be flyable.
- It should stabilize within two oscillations after a roughly 20° roll or pitch disturbance.
- The procedure should be run in a safe flight zone.
- A multicopter normally lands before applying new gains.
- Fixed-wing gains can be applied in flight and tested for 4 s, with automatic reversion if instability is detected.
- New gains must be tested carefully after tuning.

PX4 also provides a useful diagnostic based on oscillation frequency. Slow oscillations at approximately 1 Hz or below can indicate that the attitude loop is too fast relative to the rate loop; the documented correction is to reduce roll and pitch attitude P gains. Faster oscillations indicate excessive rate-loop gain, for which the rate gain is reduced. These values are troubleshooting guidance, not universal design constants.

#### ArduPilot AutoTune

ArduPilot AutoTune seeks the highest response without significant overshoot by tuning Stabilize P, rate P and D, and maximum rotational acceleration. It requires a vehicle that is already basically flyable in AltHold. The algorithm raises gains until instability is detected and then backs them off. The default `AUTOTUNE_GMBK` value reduces the final gains by 25%, creating a configurable stability margin. The `AUTOTUNE_AGGR` parameter is documented in the range 0.05–0.10; higher values produce a more aggressive tune but can produce excessive gains ([ArduPilot AutoTune documentation](https://ardupilot.org/copter/docs/autotune.html)).

ArduPilot explicitly warns that AutoTune can produce an unflyable vehicle or cause a crash when strong wind, high gyro noise, incorrect thrust-exponent calibration, flexible frames or payload mounts, flexible vibration isolation, low minimum motor spin, or overloaded motors and propellers are present. This is an important engineering qualification: an automatic tuner is not a substitute for a stable airframe, good sensors, correct actuator calibration, and an abort procedure.

#### Closed-loop autotuning and relay identification

The MathWorks multirotor example uses closed-loop PID autotuners that inject perturbations at the outputs of eight PID controllers and update their gains from measured feedback. The example tunes coupled pitch-rate and roll-rate loops sequentially and tunes other approximately decoupled loops simultaneously. It uses a 0.005 s sampling time, a bandwidth condition \(\omega T_s\leq0.3\), bandwidths of 50, 20, 5, and 1 rad/s for successive loops, and a 60° phase margin ([MathWorks cascaded UAV PID autotuning example](https://www.mathworks.com/help/slcontrol/ug/pid-controller-tuning-for-a-uav-quadcopter.html)).

The perturbation amplitude is set below 5% of the expected controller output. Too large a perturbation can destabilize the vehicle; too small a perturbation produces an inaccurate plant estimate. The example reports that the tuned multirotor completed a four-waypoint simulation in approximately 45 s, compared with nearly 150 s using baseline gains. That result is simulation evidence, although the same autotuner can also be run on hardware.

A related 2020 identification study uses a modified relay feedback test and a deep-learning classifier. It reports process identification after one steady-state relay cycle and parameter estimation in milliseconds, with simulation and experimental verification on quadrotor attitude and altitude dynamics. Its principal application is to second-order-plus-integrator-plus-time-delay models, so it is best viewed as a rapid identification method rather than evidence that all nonlinear quadrotor dynamics can be captured by one relay experiment ([MRFT and deep-learning identification](https://doi.org/10.1109/access.2020.3006277)).

### 3.3 Model-reference and estimator-based adaptation

Model-reference adaptive control (MRAC) adjusts parameters so that the measured response follows a chosen reference model. Its attraction is that it can respond to parameter changes without requiring a complete lookup table. Its risks are transient adaptation, sensitivity to excitation and noise, and the need to choose adaptation gains and projection or normalization bounds.

The variable-payload flight study described above is a concrete example. MRAC recovered from a payload drop faster than the reported gain schedule and adapted between two substantially different quadrotors using the same controller structure. The gain schedule was more reactive when the loaded state was known, while MRAC covered the full mission without initial payload information ([Diaz Luengo et al.](https://www.imavs.org/papers/2019/21.pdf)).

A 2022 CDC work integrates adaptive control into ArduPilot without altering its original architecture. Online parameter estimation is used for state-dependent and unstructured uncertainty, and tests are reported to show consistent improvement under several uncertain conditions. The supplied abstract does not provide enough numerical detail to compare error, settling time, computation, or safety margins with standard ArduPilot ([Adaptive-ArduPilot integration](https://doi.org/10.1109/cdc51059.2022.9993292)).

Cedro, Wieczorkowski, and Szcześniak use nonlinear modeling and weighted recursive least squares to identify quadcopter mass online, then make controller parameters dependent on that estimated mass. Differential filters reduce measurement noise in both identification and control, while Gauss–Newton optimization tunes the PID on the plant. The algorithms are implemented on an NI myRIO-1900 controller, so this study provides hardware implementation evidence, although it does not establish a complete broad-envelope flight benchmark ([adaptive mass-based PID study](https://doi.org/10.2478/ama-2024-0004)).

The design principle is useful: estimate the physical quantity that actually causes the plant variation, then schedule or retune gains from that estimate. Adapting directly from noisy tracking error can be simpler, but it may confuse a disturbance, sensor fault, reference change, or actuator saturation with a change in plant dynamics.

### 3.4 Fuzzy gain adaptation

Fuzzy PID uses rules such as “if error is large and error is decreasing, reduce derivative gain” or “if error is small and persistent, increase integral action.” A fuzzy inference system can output \(K_p\), \(K_i\), and \(K_d\), or their increments. It is useful when a precise plant model is unavailable but experienced control behavior can be expressed as rules.

Andrade et al. combine cascaded PID with a fuzzy module that updates gains from position error and its derivative. The implementation uses one fuzzy controller per axis and changes gains at 10 Hz through ROS/MAVLink. The method does not require a formal mathematical plant model; approximate knowledge of UAV behavior is used to define the rule base and gain ranges ([Andrade et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/2075-1702/10/1/12)).

In AirSim simulation, their fuzzy schedule reached a 1 cm position error in 6.7 s, compared with 10.8 s for the Zhao/Larson tuning approach and more than 20 s for Ziegler–Nichols. That is evidence for faster simulated position accommodation, not a direct inner attitude-loop result. The same work included a Parrot Bebop 2 altitude experiment, while the flight-control unit retained stabilization and position control. The paper reports qualitative gain adaptation and well-behaved height error, but the strongest numerical tuning comparison remains simulation-based.

Melo et al. provide a useful real-quadrotor example of the trade-off. In a fuzzy altitude scheduler, an aggressive law with \(P=1.7\), \(I=0\), \(D=0.6\) is moderated near the target by a second law with \(P=0.16\), \(I=0.009\), \(D=0.6\). In simulation, the two laws have rise times of 0.12 and 0.2, settling times of 1.0 and 1.6, and overshoots of 20% and 2%, respectively. In the physical experiment, the original and fuzzy controllers have equal reported rise time of 0.1 s, while settling time changes from 0.1 to 0.2 s and overshoot falls from 13% to 1%. The fuzzy controller also produces more observed noise, plausibly because scheduled gains amplify sensor noise ([Melo et al.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8954855/)).

This result illustrates why an improvement in one metric should not be presented as an overall victory. Fuzzy scheduling reduced overshoot substantially but increased settling time and noise in the reported experiment.

Fuzzy logic can also schedule learning gains rather than the main PID gains. Dong and He combine fuzzy PID-type iterative learning control with three learning-gain matrices. Their Lyapunov analysis establishes convergence under stated conditions, and a 45 s Gazebo trajectory simulation reports almost asymptotic convergence after 10 iterations and smaller errors than conventional PID-ILC under wind. No numerical hardware-flight benchmark is supplied in the retrieved evidence ([fuzzy PID-type iterative learning control](https://doi.org/10.3390/s19010024)).

### 3.5 Neural and fuzzy-neural PID

Neural networks can approximate a gain map, a disturbance term, or the residual between a PID command and the required control input. They can operate offline, online, or in a hybrid arrangement.

Park et al. use a multilayer fuzzy-neural network to adapt gains for both outer and inner cascaded loops. The network updates fuzzy weights and Gaussian membership parameters through gradient descent and backpropagation; the paper also gives a Lyapunov convergence analysis. The authors warn that suitable initial parameters are necessary for real-quadcopter deployment because poor initialization could cause loss of control ([PID-MFNN study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7847850/)).

In Gazebo with a 3D Robotics IRIS model and simulated 1 m/s wind, the reported square-wave computation time is 0.11444 ms for PID-MFNN and 0.11093 ms for a single-layer PID-CFNN. The square-wave RMSE values are 0.01896, 0.01902, and 0.07713 for roll, pitch, and yaw with PID-MFNN, versus 0.02698, 0.02177, and 0.07967 for PID-CFNN. For sine commands, the corresponding RMSE values are 0.0106, 0.0106, and 0.1170 versus 0.0168, 0.0154, and 0.1820. These are simulation results, and the reported computation difference is small but favors the simpler network.

The Energies study by Li et al. uses a hybrid architecture: the attitude-loop FNN is trained offline, while the position-loop FNN learns online in parallel with PID. The offline inner-loop training avoids simultaneous learning in both loops and reduces runtime computation. For a DJI Tello model, training data cover hover, waypoint following, and path tracking; five Gaussian membership functions are used per input, with up to 100 training cycles and a stopping error below 0.0001. The final reported training errors are 0.0008958 for yaw, 0.0011844 for pitch, and 0.00144 for roll ([cascade fuzzy-neural network study](https://doi.org/10.3390/en15051763)).

The same work reports lower position RMSE for the FNN-FNN controller than cascade PID in most physical experiments, but the authors identify wireless delay and force-to-remote-channel mapping as reasons why the hardware advantage was smaller than the simulation advantage. This is a useful lesson for embedded deployment: a network may approximate a controller accurately in software while the surrounding communication and actuator interface determine the real result.

### 3.6 Actor–critic and reinforcement-learning PID

Reinforcement learning can select gains, gain increments, control frequencies, or direct actuator commands. These cases should not be treated as equivalent.

Koch et al. train direct inner-loop attitude controllers with DDPG, TRPO, and PPO in the open-source GymFC simulation environment and report PPO outperforming PID. The evidence is a high-fidelity simulation evaluation for an Iris quadcopter, not a demonstrated physical-flight transfer ([Koch et al.](https://cs-web.bu.edu/faculty/richwest/papers/tcps2019.pdf)).

Sharifi and Alasty retain an incremental PID. Static gains are selected by trial and error or Ziegler–Nichols and remain fixed during a mission; an actor–critic neural structure tunes additional dynamic gains online and performs system identification. Under simulated mass uncertainty and wind gusts, the method reports lower attitude RMSE than conventional PID: roll 1.20° versus 4.49°, pitch 1.83° versus 3.85°, and yaw 0.35° versus 2.5°. The simulation uses a Gauss–Markov wind model with correlation time 0.3 and weighting factor 0.5. No physical flight test is reported in the supplied evidence ([A2CPID study](https://arxiv.org/html/2307.01312v1)).

A 2024 DDPG study compares hand-tuned, RL-tuned, and RL-estimated PID parameters for helix tracking. The full-parameter-estimation approach reports the smallest attitude and position errors in MATLAB/Simulink, with both RL methods outperforming hand tuning. Again, the result is simulation-based ([DDPG PID parameter study](https://doi.org/10.1109/icuas60882.2024.10557032)).

The 2026 RL-PID study compares PPO and SAC variants under increasing wind, payload, and sensor-noise difficulty. After 5 million training steps, all reported variants achieve position RMSE below 0.21 m under maximum disturbance, with PPO-LSTM reported as the lowest-error variant and PPO-FF as the most stable during training. The evaluated task is stable hover, not a complete attitude-manoeuvre envelope ([2026 RL-PID study](https://doi.org/10.1109/eecr69522.2026.11549405)).

Tian et al. provide one of the most technically structured examples. Their hierarchy fixes the inner attitude and angular-rate gains using LPV/LMI constraints and lets PPO tune the outer-loop gains. The actor observes tracking states and current gains, maps actions into bounded gain intervals, and applies exponential moving-average smoothing. The safety cost monitors gain-boundary, velocity, attitude, and angular-rate violations. The LMI result strictly constrains the fixed inner-loop parameters at four linearization vertices; the outer-loop policy remains protected by engineering boundaries and a Lagrangian penalty rather than a global proof ([Tian et al.](https://doi.org/10.3390/aerospace13050446)).

In high-fidelity simulation, the study reports:

- 18.5% lower overshoot in a 13 m/s step-response test;
- 50.5% shorter settling time in that test;
- 62.8% lower steady-state error;
- 9.5% shorter emergency-braking time;
- 15.0% lower velocity RMSE across 100 randomized mixed-trajectory trials;
- 40.9% lower RMSE on the chirp subset.

The study also reports approximately 9–10 μs per step for RL-PID, close to gain-scheduled PID, compared with approximately 276 μs per step for the tested linear MPC. These results are useful as a simulation comparison, but the authors identify the absence of physical-flight validation and the risk from actuator delay, sensor noise, and structural asymmetry as limitations.

The principal risks of RL-PID are therefore clear:

- training distribution may not cover the real vehicle;
- reward design can trade tracking error against safety in unintended ways;
- policies can exploit model artifacts;
- online exploration can be unsafe;
- gain changes can interact with integrator states and saturation;
- computational cost and memory may exceed a small flight controller’s budget;
- a policy may lack a formal global stability guarantee.

The safest use of RL in an open-source stack is usually as a bounded gain or scheduling layer around a validated PID baseline, with a hard fallback path, rather than as an unrestricted direct motor-command policy.

## 4. Practical enhancements that improve PID without replacing it

### 4.1 Anti-windup and actuator-saturation handling

A PID integrator accumulates error. If the actuator saturates, the commanded output cannot increase further, but the integrator may continue accumulating. When the error changes sign, the stored integral can keep the actuator saturated in the wrong direction, causing overshoot and slow recovery. This is integral windup.

The principal anti-windup methods are:

- **integrator clamping:** stop integration when the output is saturated and the error would drive it farther into saturation;
- **back-calculation:** feed the difference between unsaturated and saturated commands back into the integrator;
- **tracking mode:** force the internal controller state to follow the signal actually passed to the actuator.

MathWorks documents back-calculation and clamping and emphasizes that the saturation limits must be known. Built-in anti-windup also assumes that the PID block output is the only signal feeding the actuator; if feedforward or another command is summed afterward, the anti-windup calculation must account for the total actuator command ([MathWorks anti-windup documentation](https://www.mathworks.com/help/simulink/slref/anti-windup-control-using-a-pid-controller.html)).

PX4 limits integral authority and normally limits control-allocation outputs to approximately \(-1\) to \(1\). ArduPilot limits the rate-controller integral contribution with axis-specific I-max parameters. These limits are not optional cosmetic features: they define how the controller behaves when the physical vehicle cannot produce the requested torque ([PX4 controller architecture](https://docs.px4.io/main/en/flight_stack/controller_diagrams), [ArduPilot helicopter rate controller](https://ardupilot.org/copter/docs/traditional-helicopter-control-system.html)).

Mixer saturation needs its own logic. PX4’s Airmode can preserve attitude and rate tracking at low or zero throttle by boosting thrust, while disabling Airmode reduces torque to keep motor commands feasible. Upper saturation prevents any motor from exceeding 100% command, but Airmode can cause ascent at zero throttle if excessive gains generate oscillation. Therefore, Airmode should be enabled only after the basic tune is sound ([PX4 Airmode and mixer saturation](https://docs.px4.io/main/en/config_mc/pid_tuning_guide_multicopter)).

A sound implementation should log:

- unsaturated PID output;
- saturated actuator output;
- integrator state;
- saturation duration;
- mixer scaling;
- available thrust margin;
- whether Airmode or equivalent allocation logic was active.

Without these signals, a poor tune can be mistaken for a gain problem when the real problem is unavailable actuator authority.

### 4.2 Derivative filtering and sensor-noise management

The derivative term provides damping, but it magnifies measurement noise. PX4 places the derivative action on the feedback path to avoid derivative kick and applies a low-pass filter. Its tuning guide warns that excessive D gain makes motors twitchy or hot, while insufficient D produces overshoot ([PX4 multicopter PID tuning guide](https://docs.px4.io/main/en/config_mc/pid_tuning_guide_multicopter)).

Good derivative practice includes:

- differentiate a measured rate or filtered measurement rather than a noisy attitude command;
- use derivative-on-measurement or derivative-on-feedback to avoid setpoint kick;
- choose the filter cutoff from measured vibration and the desired phase margin;
- avoid differentiating a signal whose delay is already large;
- use identical and documented filter behavior in simulation and hardware;
- monitor the D contribution and motor temperature where possible.

The filter is a compromise. A cutoff that is too high passes vibration into the motors; a cutoff that is too low adds phase lag and reduces achievable rate-loop bandwidth. The correct value depends on IMU noise, vibration, sample time, motor response, and the desired rate-loop bandwidth.

The variable-payload study by Diaz Luengo et al. omitted derivative terms from its position and velocity cascade because OptiTrack noise made derivative action unreliable. This does not mean derivative action should always be removed from attitude control; it shows that a derivative term is useful only when the measurement and filtering support it ([variable-payload study](https://www.imavs.org/papers/2019/21.pdf)).

### 4.3 Feedforward and reference shaping

Feedforward supplies a command based on the desired motion rather than waiting for feedback error. In a rate loop, a desired angular-rate or angular-acceleration feedforward term can reduce the feedback effort required to follow a command. In an attitude loop, reference body-rate feedforward can remove the lag of a pure proportional attitude law.

PX4 smooths multicopter attitude setpoints with a second-order critically damped reference model and feeds the model’s reference body rate forward to the rate setpoint. Its documentation states that this removes the pure-P law’s steady-state tracking lag. The feedforward is scaled by `MC_REF_FF`, clipped by `MC_REF_FF_MAX`, and combined with rate-command saturation ([PX4 controller diagrams](https://docs.px4.io/main/en/flight_stack/controller_diagrams)).

ArduPilot exposes body-frame rate feedforward that allows rate targets to bypass some P/I action for a sharper response ([ArduPilot attitude architecture](https://deepwiki.com/ArduPilot/ardupilot/2.3-attitude-and-position-control)). ArduPilot’s helicopter controller also combines input-rate feedforward with PID rate feedback: feedforward provides the baseline actuator command, while P, I, and D correct disturbances and model error ([ArduPilot helicopter rate controller](https://ardupilot.org/copter/docs/traditional-helicopter-control-system.html)).

Feedforward reduces the work assigned to the integral term. A 2024 quadrotor study specifically proposes adding feedforward to PID to reduce integral saturation and reports lower PID and integral output, faster action, and lower error. Its supplied abstract does not provide enough information to quantify the improvement across a standardized attitude benchmark ([feedforward-augmented quadrotor PID](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3679409.3679465)).

Feedforward is not automatically robust. If the actuator model or desired-motion estimate is wrong, it can inject error. It should therefore be bounded, filtered where necessary, and disabled or reduced when estimator quality is poor.

### 4.4 Thrust-model and actuator compensation

A PID controller can be well tuned while the actuator map is wrong. The motor mixer may assume that a normalized command produces a particular thrust, but the actual thrust depends on propeller, motor, ESC, battery voltage, air density, and operating point.

PX4 recommends thrust-stand measurement when possible. If no thrust stand is available, it suggests empirical adjustment of the thrust-model factor: starting at 0.3 and increasing by 0.1, observing whether oscillations occur at low or high throttle. The exact value is platform-specific, and changing it may require rate retuning ([PX4 thrust-curve compensation](https://docs.px4.io/main/en/config_mc/pid_tuning_guide_multicopter)).

The F450 implementation by Burggräf et al. builds a motor-behavior table from measured motor, PWM, and microcontroller data, then derives an RPM-to-thrust model. This is an actuator-characterization table rather than a gain schedule, but it can support feedforward and improve the validity of model-based tuning ([Burggräf et al.](https://protech.mb.uni-siegen.de/ipem/download/Quadrotors%20in%20factory%20applications%20design%20and%20implementation.pdf)).

### 4.5 Disturbance observers and compensation

A disturbance observer estimates forces, torques, or lumped model error and feeds the estimate forward into the controller. It can improve disturbance rejection without changing the basic PID structure.

The main families are:

- nonlinear disturbance observers (NDOs);
- extended-state observers (ESOs);
- reduced-order observers;
- adaptive estimators;
- neural-network and fuzzy disturbance approximators;
- external force and torque estimators.

The 2024 survey distinguishes model-based NDO/ESO methods from model-independent adaptive, neural, and fuzzy methods. NDO and ESO use a mathematical model to estimate disturbances; neural and fuzzy methods use tracking errors or other measured signals and can operate with less model information ([disturbance-observer and adaptive-control survey](https://doi.org/10.3390/act13060217)).

A reduced-order ESO-based nonlinear PID design uses IMU angular velocity to estimate lumped disturbance and applies the estimate as feedforward compensation. The study includes payload-induced disturbances and sensor noise in numerical and quadrotor-platform experiments, but the supplied evidence does not provide common tracking-error numbers ([reduced-order ESO nonlinear PID](https://doi.org/10.3390/pr13051470)).

Observer bandwidth must be selected carefully. The survey gives a representative NDO condition \(l(v)>1/2\) for convergence under its stated assumptions and says observer error dynamics should be faster than the closed-loop dynamics. That is a theoretical condition for the cited observer, not a universal flight-controller gain. Increasing observer bandwidth can improve disturbance tracking but also amplify sensor noise and phase lag.

The Processes study notes that full-order observers can introduce phase lag and high-frequency noise sensitivity in high-bandwidth UAVs, and that experimental validation under realistic noisy and dynamic conditions remains sparse. A reduced-order observer can be attractive when only a measured angular rate and a limited model are available.

External-force compensation can also be combined with learned control. In a DCRL study, acceleration and attitude are used to estimate external force, a 30 Hz low-pass filter reduces rotor-vibration and IMU noise, and the compensation is tested on a PixRacer vehicle in indoor and outdoor flight. Under a 3.6 m/s indoor wind, position-error mean falls from 8.4 cm for the uncompensated RL controller to 2 cm for the disturbance-compensated controller. This is evidence for the observer and filter architecture, but it is not a direct comparison of inner attitude PID performance ([disturbance-compensated RL flight study](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/11/7/3257)).

### 4.6 Latency, sampling, and actuator dynamics

The rate loop is usually the fastest loop, so latency consumes a larger fraction of its phase margin. The total delay includes:

- IMU sampling and digital filtering;
- estimator computation;
- control-loop scheduling;
- communication;
- mixer and actuator computation;
- ESC and motor response;
- logging or transport delays.

The MathWorks example uses a 0.005 s sample time and requires \(\omega T_s\leq0.3\), which caps the autotuner’s bandwidth at 60 rad/s; it selects 50 rad/s for the inner pitch and roll rate loops. This illustrates a sampled-data constraint rather than a universal rule ([MathWorks UAV PID tuning example](https://www.mathworks.com/help/slcontrol/ug/pid-controller-tuning-for-a-uav-quadcopter.html)).

A 2023 dynamic-surface/UDE study warns that ignoring first-order-plus-time-delay actuator dynamics can significantly deteriorate performance or cause instability because controller bandwidth must respect actuator dynamics ([UDE attitude tracking study](https://doi.org/10.3390/drones7050305)). A 2026 fuzzy Padé study uses tracking error, error rate, and a delay estimate to adjust a delay approximation with two constant-time intermediate state changes. Its advantages are reported under its bounded-delay assumptions; the study is not a universal replacement for delay identification ([fuzzy Padé delay compensation](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-45781-x)).

In practical PID tuning, delay should be measured or conservatively bounded before increasing rate-loop gain. If a controller oscillates only when a wireless link, high-order filter, or external estimator is enabled, retuning gains alone may hide rather than solve the problem.

## 5. How to select PID parameters optimally

### 5.1 “Optimal” means constrained and mission-specific

There is no single globally optimal PID parameter vector for every UAV, payload, flight condition, and mission. An optimum is defined relative to:

- a particular vehicle and actuator configuration;
- an operating envelope;
- a reference-command class;
- a disturbance set;
- sensor and delay characteristics;
- actuator and attitude constraints;
- an objective weighting.

For a cascaded attitude controller, a useful conceptual objective is

$$J(K)=w_e\int e^2(t)\,dt+w_1\int |e(t)|\,dt+w_t\int t|e(t)|\,dt+w_u\int u^2(t)\,dt+w_{\Delta u}\int \dot{u}^2(t)\,dt+P_{\mathrm{sat}}+P_{\mathrm{viol}}.$$

The terms correspond to squared error, integral absolute error, time-weighted absolute error, control effort, command variation, saturation, and safety violations. The weights must be normalized because angle error, angular-rate error, torque, and actuator command have different units and scales.

The objective should usually be evaluated over multiple scenarios rather than a single nominal step:

- hover and low-thrust operation;
- high-thrust or high-speed operation;
- minimum and maximum battery voltage;
- empty and loaded configurations;
- positive and negative roll/pitch commands;
- yaw-rate commands;
- wind or external torque;
- sensor-noise and delay variations;
- actuator saturation and command-rate limits.

A weighted average rewards typical conditions. A worst-case or percentile objective protects the envelope. A Pareto front exposes the trade-off between error, speed, overshoot, and effort instead of hiding it in one arbitrary scalar.

### 5.2 A practical tuning sequence for cascaded loops

The order matters because the outer loop treats the inner loop as part of its plant.

#### 1. Characterize the hardware before tuning

Measure or estimate:

- total mass and center of gravity;
- \(I_x\), \(I_y\), and \(I_z\);
- arm length and motor/propeller coefficients;
- thrust and torque versus command and voltage;
- motor and ESC response time;
- sensor sample rates and filters;
- estimator and communication delay;
- mixer limits and actuator slew limits;
- vibration and IMU noise.

The MOPSO study by Gomez et al. uses measured mass, inertia, and motor thrust/torque relationships as model inputs. It obtains inertia with a pendulum method and fits polynomial thrust and torque functions from motor tests. The authors note that gains computed from a nominal model are reliable only for small model-parameter variations unless robustness is deliberately included ([Gomez et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/2226-4310/7/6/71)).

#### 2. Establish safe initial gains

Use a validated tune from a similar vehicle only as a starting point. PX4 explicitly recommends using gains from a vehicle with similar size and inertia and then adjusting platform-specific parameters. Default gains are intentionally conservative, so acceptable flight does not necessarily imply good tracking ([PX4 multicopter tuning guide](https://docs.px4.io/main/en/config_mc/pid_tuning_guide_multicopter)).

Before a flight test, verify that the vehicle can stabilize from small disturbances. PX4 requires stabilization within two oscillations at approximately 20° before autotuning. ArduPilot similarly requires a basically flyable vehicle before AutoTune. If the vehicle cannot stabilize, an optimizer or adaptive law should not be allowed to explore freely.

#### 3. Tune the inner angular-rate loop first

The rate loop directly controls the fast rotational dynamics. Tune roll and pitch P and D first, then add the minimum integral action needed to remove persistent rate offsets. Yaw often uses a different D strategy because yaw dynamics and sensor noise differ.

A typical manual sequence is:

- apply a bounded rate step;
- increase P until the response is fast but just below sustained oscillation;
- add D until overshoot is adequately damped without excessive noise;
- add I until persistent offsets disappear without slow oscillation;
- repeat for both signs and multiple throttle levels;
- check actuator saturation and motor temperature.

PX4 recommends increasing gains by 20–30% per iteration initially and reducing changes to 5–10% for final refinement, with the vehicle landed before parameter changes. These increments are procedural guidance, not universal gain values ([PX4 multicopter tuning guide](https://docs.px4.io/main/en/config_mc/pid_tuning_guide_multicopter)).

#### 4. Tune the outer attitude loop second

Once the rate loop is stable and sufficiently fast, tune the attitude P gain gradually. The outer loop should command a rate that the inner loop can follow without saturation. If the outer gain is too high relative to the rate-loop bandwidth, slow attitude oscillations can appear even though the rate loop is individually stable.

For many multicopter attitude cascades, the outer attitude loop uses P rather than a full PID because the inner rate-loop integral and the vehicle’s attitude response can already remove the relevant steady-state error. Adding another integrator should be justified by a persistent attitude bias that cannot be corrected elsewhere, and it must be protected against saturation.

#### 5. Tune velocity and position loops afterward

Although the question concerns attitude control, outer position and velocity loops generate the attitude setpoints. They must be tuned after the attitude cascade because their plant includes the already closed attitude response. Position-loop tuning can otherwise be misdiagnosed as attitude-loop instability.

MathWorks tunes coupled pitch-rate and roll-rate loops sequentially, then pitch and roll attitude loops, then paired velocity loops and position loops. Its sequence is pitch rate, roll rate, pitch and roll, x/y velocity, and x/y position ([MathWorks UAV PID tuning example](https://www.mathworks.com/help/slcontrol/ug/pid-controller-tuning-for-a-uav-quadcopter.html)).

### 5.3 Bandwidth separation and stability margins

The inner loop must be faster than the outer loop. If their bandwidths are too close, the outer loop commands a plant whose transient response is still changing, producing interaction and possible oscillation. If the separation is excessive, the inner loop may demand bandwidth that the motor, sensor, sample time, or actuator cannot support.

The MathWorks example uses:

- 50 rad/s for pitch and roll rate;
- 20 rad/s for pitch and roll attitude;
- 5 rad/s for x/y velocity;
- 1 rad/s for x/y position;
- 60° phase margin for each loop.

A 2022 Sensors study reports an attitude-to-position frequency ratio of approximately 5–10, with higher attitude frequency improving stability but slowing waypoint following. A generic cascade-design example by Wang gives an inner bandwidth of 50 and outer bandwidth of 0.2, a 250:1 ratio, but explicitly treats the ratio as a general cascade principle rather than a universal UAV setting ([MathWorks example](https://www.mathworks.com/help/slcontrol/ug/pid-controller-tuning-for-a-uav-quadcopter.html), [Sensors frequency study](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8220/22/1/150), [Wang cascade-design example](https://www.ifac2020.org/fileadmin/public/Redaktion/Dokumente/Workshopslides/Slides_Workshop_Wang.pdf)).

These values should therefore be treated as reference points. The actual separation should be selected from identified plant bandwidth, actuator delay, sensor noise, and desired phase margin. A high rate-loop bandwidth is not beneficial if it is dominated by delay or vibration.

### 5.4 Classical and analytical tuning

#### Ziegler–Nichols and relay methods

Ziegler–Nichols ultimate-gain tuning increases P gain until sustained oscillation, measures ultimate gain and period, and calculates PID parameters. It is simple and can provide an initial tune, but it is intentionally close to an oscillatory boundary. A quadrotor’s actuator saturation, delay, coupling, and noise make the method risky as a final procedure.

A quadrotor study explicitly notes that Ziegler–Nichols can produce oscillatory responses and overshoot and cannot perform online parameter tuning ([Park et al.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7847850/)). Andrade et al. report more than 20 s to reach a 1 cm accommodation criterion with Ziegler–Nichols in their AirSim position simulation, although that comparison is task-specific ([Andrade et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/2075-1702/10/1/12)).

Relay feedback and modified relay tests can be safer if the amplitude is bounded and the vehicle is already stable. The relay experiment should be performed in a safe operating region, and the identified model should be validated against a separate response before gains are applied.

#### Direct synthesis and IAE

Bolandi et al. use a hover-linearized quadrotor model, direct synthesis, and a desired closed-loop time constant. The time constant is selected by trading response speed and disturbance rejection against stability, robustness, and sensitivity to parameter variation. Integral absolute error is used as the objective, and a genetic algorithm selects the time constant. The study reports faster simulated disturbance rejection than a backstepping comparison, but also notes that the fast response produces overshoot ([Bolandi et al.](https://file.scirp.org/Html/12-7900231_35654.htm)).

This illustrates a useful analytical approach: reduce the search to physically meaningful parameters such as desired bandwidth or time constant, then optimize those parameters under robustness constraints. It is usually more interpretable than searching all gains without structure.

#### PX4 and ArduPilot autotune

Autotuning is attractive because it replaces manual trial-and-error with measured system response. Its quality depends on excitation amplitude, signal-to-noise ratio, model structure, airframe flexibility, and safety gating. PX4’s low-order uncoupled model is appropriate for supported vehicles within its assumptions, but not a guarantee for highly coupled or flexible frames. ArduPilot’s instability-detection and gain-backoff logic provides a practical margin but still requires a flyable vehicle and safe test conditions.

### 5.5 Model-based and robust tuning

A model-based method can produce gains more systematically than manual tuning, provided the model includes the important dynamics.

A useful model hierarchy is:

1. rigid-body rotational dynamics;
2. motor and ESC response;
3. thrust and torque nonlinearity;
4. sensor filtering and delay;
5. mixer saturation and command slew;
6. aerodynamic drag and coupling;
7. payload and battery uncertainty.

The controller can then be tuned at one operating point, across a grid of local models, or directly with robust constraints. A hover-local model is adequate for hover if its limitations are accepted. It is not adequate for a large high-speed envelope without additional scheduling or robust analysis.

LPV/LMI methods are useful when a designer needs explicit stability or disturbance-attenuation constraints. Kazemi and Tarighi use PID-based LPV modeling and LMI-computed gains to guarantee an \(H_\infty\) attenuation level in simulation. Tian et al. use common Lyapunov and phase/gain-margin constraints to define a safe domain for an adaptive outer-loop search. The latter explicitly limits its guarantee to the fixed inner-loop parameters and selected LPV vertices.

Robust analysis is especially valuable for screening candidate PID gains. Before performance optimization, reject any candidate that:

- has an unstable local closed loop;
- violates the required phase or gain margin;
- exceeds actuator authority;
- saturates for the nominal reference;
- amplifies sensor noise excessively;
- fails under the specified parameter uncertainty;
- causes gain transitions or integrator jumps.

### 5.6 Metaheuristic and multiobjective optimization

Genetic algorithms, particle swarm optimization, differential evolution, grey-wolf optimization, and Bayesian optimization can search PID gains when the objective is nonlinear, nonconvex, or only available through simulation.

The most important design choice is not the algorithm name but the evaluation function. An optimizer that minimizes only RMSE may select gains with unacceptable overshoot, actuator saturation, motor heating, or noise sensitivity. A useful optimization loop should simulate each candidate under multiple conditions and apply hard rejection or penalty for safety violations.

Gomez et al. use multiobjective particle swarm optimization with a Pareto front containing overshoot, rise time, and RMSE. The optimization is applied to the PX4 controller structure and uses mass, inertia, and motor thrust/torque data. The study also adds an oscillation-hazard objective based on frequency-domain analysis and evaluates model perturbations of ±15% in mass, inertia, geometry, and propulsion coefficients. The resulting gains are tested experimentally on a quadrotor, including tethered roll and pitch tests, yaw-rate testing, and free-flight altitude testing ([Gomez et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/2226-4310/7/6/71)).

The reported experimental results include:

- roll overshoot of 10.5163%, rise time of 0.1448 s, and RMSE of 2.0341%;
- pitch overshoot of 5.7190%, rise time of 0.2248 s, and RMSE of 1.7792%;
- yaw overshoot of 4.6268%, rise time of 0.3176 s, and RMSE of 1.6963%;
- altitude RMSE of 0.3397 m, with rise-time and overshoot fields unavailable in the reported table.

These numbers belong to that vehicle, controller parameterization, test fixture, and measurement definition. They should not be copied as target values for another UAV.

The MOPSO approach is valuable because it exposes trade-offs. A designer can select a conservative Pareto solution with low overshoot and control effort, or a more aggressive solution with faster rise time. It still does not prove global optimality, and it can optimize the wrong behavior if the model or objective is incomplete.

A 2025 simulation framework compares metaheuristics, Bayesian optimization, and DRL for cascade-PID selection. It reports Grey Wolf Optimization as best in that setup, Bayesian optimization as sample-efficient but more expensive per iteration and dependent on the design domain, and DRL below the manual Ziegler–Nichols baseline in the reported configuration ([2025 cascade-PID optimization study](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.17423v1)). This is a useful warning against ranking algorithms by reputation. Results depend on model fidelity, search bounds, reward design, trajectory set, and constraints.

### 5.7 Online refinement

Online refinement should be slower and more constrained than the flight-control loop. A practical online tuner should:

- begin from a validated baseline;
- update only when the estimator and sensors are healthy;
- enforce explicit gain bounds;
- limit gain rate of change;
- freeze adaptation during severe saturation or faults;
- use filtered errors and persistent excitation;
- preserve or smoothly transform integral states;
- detect divergence or oscillation;
- revert to the baseline when confidence falls.

The 2026 safety-constrained RL-PID study uses separate actor and safety-multiplier time scales, gain-domain mapping, and exponential smoothing. This is a good pattern for bounded adaptation, but its guarantees remain conditional on the model and safety domain. An online tuner should not be described as “globally stable” merely because its gains are clipped.

## 6. Comparative evidence, metrics, and validation

### 6.1 Method comparison on shared engineering axes

The following comparison uses the available evidence without treating incomparable experiments as a single benchmark.

| Method family | Operating-condition coverage | Tracking and disturbance behavior | Safety, computation, and tuning burden | Evidence level |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fixed cascaded PID with safeguards | Strong near the tuned condition; limited under payload, speed, voltage, and major disturbance changes | Fast and effective when well tuned; can become sluggish, oscillatory, or windup-prone outside the local condition | Lowest computation and easiest certification; requires careful manual or automatic tuning and protection logic | Widely deployed in PX4, ArduPilot, and other stacks; many flight implementations, but no common cross-condition baseline |
| Lookup-table or gain-scheduled PID | Good when the scheduling variables are measurable and the table covers the envelope | Smooth interpolation can improve speed and disturbance rejection across known regimes; incorrect scheduling can be worse than fixed gains | Low runtime cost; requires local models, tables, transition logic, and reliable scheduling measurements | Fixed-wing wind-tunnel evidence, variable-payload flight evidence, and firmware examples; quantitative coverage remains platform-specific |
| LPV or multi-model PID | Potentially broad over a defined parameter envelope | Can retain margins across operating points when common constraints are satisfied | Higher offline modeling and LMI cost; runtime interpolation is moderate; formal guarantees depend on the model and vertices | Mostly simulation; some simulation-and-experiment LPV evidence, but no common flight benchmark |
| MRAC or estimator-based adaptive PID | Responds to unlisted payload or parameter changes if adaptation remains bounded | Can recover from payload changes and model uncertainty; transients depend on adaptation gains | Moderate runtime cost; requires normalization, projection, estimator quality, and stability analysis | Variable-payload flight evidence for MRAC versus scheduling; detailed universal metrics unavailable |
| Fuzzy PID | Broad qualitative adaptation from error and error rate without a precise model | Can reduce overshoot and accommodate nonlinear behavior; may increase noise, settling time, or chattering | Moderate computation; rule, membership, and gain-range design are labor-intensive | Simulation plus altitude/position flight tests; direct inner-attitude flight comparisons are limited |
| Neural or fuzzy-neural PID | Can represent nonlinear gain maps and disturbance compensation if training data cover the envelope | Often improves simulated RMSE and transient response; sensitive to delay, mapping, initialization, and unseen conditions | Higher memory and computation; online learning needs bounds and fallback | Gazebo and MATLAB evidence, plus Tello and other hardware experiments mainly for position/altitude |
| Observer- or feedforward-enhanced PID | Extends coverage for measured or estimated wind, drag, payload, and actuator effects | Usually improves rejection of persistent disturbances and reduces integral demand | Observer bandwidth, model error, noise, and phase lag must be controlled; moderate computation | Strong theoretical and simulation literature; selected platform experiments, but no common PID ablation benchmark |
| Offline optimized fixed PID | Optimizes a specified model and objective, often more repeatably than manual tuning | Can improve overshoot, rise time, RMSE, or control effort at nominal and perturbed conditions | No runtime learning cost; offline search can be expensive and results depend on model and objectives | MOPSO PX4 study includes simulation, parameter perturbation, and experimental validation |
| RL gain or frequency adaptation | Potentially broad and task-dependent, including wind, payload, and trajectory changes | Can improve dynamic tracking in simulation; results are highly setup-sensitive | Highest training and validation burden; inference can be moderate, but online exploration is safety-critical | Mostly simulation; some physical RL and observer-compensation flights, but no standardized RL-PID attitude benchmark |

### 6.2 What the measured studies actually show

#### Gain scheduling versus adaptive control in flight

The variable-payload flight study is one of the clearest direct comparisons. It shows that gain scheduling is effective when the payload state is known and switching is nearly immediate, while MRAC is more broadly adaptive and recovers faster in the reported drop mission. Neither result supports a universal ranking. The choice depends on whether the scheduling state is measurable, whether the operating modes are repeatable, and whether the mission permits adaptation transients.

The Concordia fault-tolerance study reaches a similar conditional conclusion. Gain-scheduled PID reacts faster than MRAC to maintain height after actuator faults when switching time is close to zero. If transition detection or gain application is delayed, the advantage is reduced ([Concordia study](https://doi.org/10.21535/dj2zd771)).

#### Fuzzy scheduling and the transient trade-off

Melo et al. demonstrate a substantial overshoot reduction in real altitude control, from 13% to 1%, while settling time increases from 0.1 to 0.2 s and observed noise increases. The result supports fuzzy scheduling as a way to change transient priorities, not as evidence that fuzzy logic improves every metric simultaneously ([Melo et al.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8954855/)).

Andrade et al. report faster AirSim accommodation with fuzzy gain scheduling, but their text contains an internal contradiction about the comparison with ArduPilot: one sentence says ArduPilot has shorter accommodation, while another says the proposed controller is 1.5 s faster. That numerical advantage should therefore not be treated as settled. The broader result—that the proposed method performs well in simulation and that the Parrot Bebop altitude experiment demonstrates physical integration—is still useful, but the conflicting comparison limits the strength of the ranking claim ([Andrade et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/2075-1702/10/1/12)).

#### Neural and actor–critic methods

The neural studies generally report improvements over simpler neural or fixed-PID baselines in simulation. Park et al. report lower RMSE for PID-MFNN than PID-CFNN under square and sine commands, with only a small computation-time increase. Li et al. report lower position RMSE for FNN-assisted control in most physical experiments, but also identify communication delay and command mapping as sources of performance loss.

The actor–critic PID study reports large simulated RMSE reductions under mass and wind uncertainty, but no flight test. These results are promising for adaptive gain generation, but they do not establish robustness to simultaneous payload, wind, sensor noise, delay, and actuator saturation on a common embedded platform.

#### RL and frequency scheduling

The CFA/QFP study demonstrates that even the ratio between attitude and position control frequencies can be state-dependent. In Crazyflie simulation, CFA+QFP outperforms fixed-frequency PID under circular and linear wind, while CFA without the future predictor performs worse than conventional PID. This is evidence that an adaptation signal is essential; adaptation without reliable disturbance information can degrade performance ([CFA and QFP study](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8220/22/1/150)).

The 2026 safety-constrained RL-PID study offers detailed simulation statistics and a computation comparison, but its own limitations state that the work has not yet closed the sim-to-real gap. The reported improvement is therefore strong evidence for the simulated architecture and objective, not a flight-certified result.

### 6.3 Metrics must retain their context

A useful result must state:

- the controlled variable: attitude angle, angular rate, velocity, altitude, or position;
- the controller being compared;
- the reference signal;
- the disturbance and its magnitude;
- the vehicle model or platform;
- the sampling and delay conditions;
- the metric definition and units;
- the number of trials and variability.

For example, a 15% velocity-RMSE reduction in 100 mixed simulated trajectories is not directly comparable with a 1% altitude overshoot in one real flight or a 2° attitude-RMSE result under a simulated Gauss–Markov wind. These results answer different questions.

The most useful metrics for attitude PID evaluation are:

- angle RMSE, MAE, IAE, or ITAE;
- body-rate RMSE and peak error;
- rise time;
- settling time with an explicit tolerance band;
- overshoot and undershoot;
- disturbance-recovery time;
- maximum attitude and angular rate;
- actuator saturation percentage and duration;
- control effort and command slew;
- motor temperature or current where available;
- noise amplification;
- phase and gain margins;
- computation time, memory, and deadline misses;
- gain-transition amplitude and rate;
- failure, abort, or reversion rate.

A single step response is insufficient for a changing-flight-state problem. The test set should include both positive and negative commands, multiple amplitudes, different throttle levels, varying payload, battery voltage, and disturbances.

### 6.4 Simulation, HIL, and flight evidence

Simulation is valuable for broad parameter sweeps and unsafe conditions, but it can conceal actuator delay, sensor bias, vibration, estimator failure, communication timing, and structural flexibility. A controller that wins in simulation can lose on hardware because its gains exploit an ideal model.

Hardware-in-the-loop places the real embedded controller in a real-time simulated plant with electrical emulation of sensors and actuators. Louali et al. describe HIL as a way to test an embedded controller with realistic real-time inputs and outputs before field deployment, reducing development time and flight-test risk ([quadrotor HIL architecture](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10425854)). The supplied evidence supports HIL as a validation stage, but it does not provide a populated common HIL comparison of fixed, scheduled, adaptive, fuzzy, neural, and RL-PID controllers.
