Physical-flight evidence is uneven:

- PX4 and ArduPilot autotune documentation demonstrates deployable procedures and safety logic, but not a controlled academic head-to-head benchmark.
- Poksawat et al. report wind-tunnel implementation of fixed-wing gain scheduling.
- Diaz Luengo et al. report real variable-payload flights comparing MRAC and gain scheduling.
- Melo et al. report a real altitude-control experiment with fuzzy scheduling.
- Gomez et al. report experimental tests of MOPSO-tuned PX4 gains, including tethered attitude tests.
- Andrade et al. integrate fuzzy gain tuning with real UAV altitude control, while their strongest numerical comparisons are simulated.
- Park and Li et al. provide primarily simulation or position/altitude evidence for neural methods.
- Direct neural and RL-PID attitude results under simultaneous payload, wind, noise, and delay remain sparse.
- The retrieved RL-PID studies do not establish physical-flight superiority over a well-tuned fixed or gain-scheduled PID on a shared attitude benchmark.

### 6.5 Why no universal ranking follows

The available sources do not provide one standardized experiment in which every requested alternative—fixed PID, gain-scheduled PID, adaptive PID, fuzzy PID, neural PID, and RL-PID—is run on the same UAV with the same disturbances, metrics, actuator limits, and compute budget. Therefore, a universal ranking would be manufactured rather than measured.

The evidence supports conditional judgments:

- fixed PID is usually best for simplicity, transparency, and low computation near a well-defined operating point;
- gain scheduling is attractive when the dominant operating variable is measurable and repeatable;
- MRAC or bounded adaptive estimation is valuable when the plant changes online and the change is not known in advance;
- fuzzy PID is practical when a useful rule base can be written and moderate computation is available;
- neural PID can represent complex nonlinear maps but requires representative data, initialization protection, and compute;
- RL-PID can optimize task-dependent adaptation but currently has the highest validation and safety burden;
- observer and feedforward enhancements often provide a better first improvement than replacing the entire PID structure.

## 7. Recommendations for open-source flight controllers

### 7.1 Recommended default

For most open-source multicopter projects, the deployable baseline should remain a well-tuned cascaded rate-and-attitude PID with:

- a validated actuator and thrust model;
- inner rate-loop tuning before outer attitude tuning;
- derivative-on-feedback and low-pass filtering;
- bounded integral action with anti-windup;
- explicit mixer and actuator saturation handling;
- rate and attitude setpoint limits;
- body-rate or reference-model feedforward;
- voltage and thrust compensation where necessary;
- high-rate logging of errors, integrators, commands, saturation, and timing;
- an autotune procedure with readiness checks, gain backoff, and reversion.

This combination addresses many real failures before a more complex adaptive method is introduced. It also provides the baseline against which an enhancement must be judged.

### 7.2 When to choose gain scheduling

Use a lookup table, scaling law, or LPV schedule when:

- the operating variation is known in advance;
- a reliable scheduling variable is available;
- local gains can be tuned and validated;
- transitions can be interpolated or rate-limited;
- a fallback gain set exists.

Suitable examples include:

- airspeed scaling for fixed-wing control;
- throttle or voltage scheduling for racing or high-thrust multirotors;
- payload-class or estimated-mass scheduling;
- velocity-dependent LPV scheduling for aggressive flight;
- different gains for known flight modes or actuator configurations.

The scheduler should be conservative when the variable is uncertain. If payload estimation is unreliable, it is safer to use overlapping gain regions with hysteresis and a robust baseline than to switch sharply between inaccurate tables.

### 7.3 When to choose online adaptive or self-tuning PID

Use bounded online adaptation when:

- the vehicle’s mass, inertia, actuator effectiveness, or disturbance environment changes during flight;
- the change cannot be represented adequately by a fixed table;
- an adaptation signal can be measured with sufficient quality;
- gain bounds and a reversion path can be enforced.

MRAC, recursive mass estimation, or adaptive ArduPilot-style parameter estimation are reasonable candidates for payload changes. Autotune is appropriate for commissioning or controlled recalibration, not unrestricted continual experimentation during a mission.

Online updates should be slower than the rate loop, filtered, bounded, and suspended during poor estimator quality or sustained actuator saturation.

### 7.4 When to choose fuzzy PID

Fuzzy gain scheduling is suitable when:

- a precise dynamic model is unavailable;
- experienced operators can express useful rules;
- error and error rate provide a meaningful indication of the required response;
- the embedded processor can execute the rule base;
- gain ranges and derivative signals are well filtered.

The rules should explicitly account for both large-error transients and small-error noise. Integral action should be gated or limited near saturation. The fuzzy outputs should be rate-limited to prevent gain chattering. The Melo and Andrade results show why overshoot, settling time, and noise must be evaluated together.

### 7.5 When to choose neural or reinforcement-learning PID

Use neural or RL gain adaptation only when the project can provide:

- a sufficiently representative training distribution;
- a realistic actuator, sensor, and delay model;
- explicit gain, attitude, rate, and actuator constraints;
- deterministic runtime and memory bounds;
- a validated fallback controller;
- simulation, HIL, and staged flight testing;
- monitoring for out-of-distribution states;
- a rollback or freeze mechanism.

A sensible architecture is to retain fixed inner rate gains and let a learned policy adjust bounded outer-loop gains, as in the LPV/LMI-constrained RL-PID study. This limits the learned policy’s authority over the fastest and most safety-critical dynamics. Direct neural motor control should require substantially stronger evidence than a gain-scheduling policy.

### 7.6 A practical parameter-selection policy

The following policy answers how PID parameters should be selected in practice:

1. Measure or estimate mass, inertia, motor response, thrust mapping, voltage dependence, sensor noise, and delay.

2. Define the operating envelope, reference commands, disturbances, actuator limits, and safety constraints before selecting gains.

3. Tune the inner roll, pitch, and yaw rate loops first, using measured rate steps and a bandwidth compatible with sample time, filtering, motor response, and phase-margin requirements.

4. Tune the outer attitude P loops only after the rate loops are stable and faster, using bounded attitude steps and checking both signs, amplitudes, saturation, and recovery.

5. Add anti-windup, derivative filtering, feedforward, reference shaping, mixer handling, and thrust-model compensation before judging the gain set.

6. Use classical or autotune methods to obtain a safe initial point, then refine with a plant model, multiobjective optimization, or a local operating-point table.

7. If the vehicle operates across repeatable regimes, schedule gains or controller outputs using measured variables and smooth transitions.

8. If the dynamics change unpredictably, use bounded adaptive estimation, MRAC, an observer, fuzzy adaptation, or a constrained learning layer rather than assuming one fixed gain set will remain optimal.

9. Validate candidate gains against nonlinear simulation, parameter uncertainty, sensor noise, latency, actuator saturation, HIL where available, and staged flight tests.

10. Select the final gains or schedule from the best safe trade-off, not from the smallest nominal RMSE alone.

The resulting controller is “optimal” only relative to the stated envelope and objective. A gain set with the smallest step-response settling time may be inferior if it saturates motors, amplifies IMU noise, loses phase margin under delay, or performs poorly with a payload.

## Closing judgment

The best way to improve practical UAV PID performance is usually not to discard PID immediately. Start with the cascaded architecture used by PX4 and ArduPilot, make the actuator, sensor, timing, filtering, feedforward, anti-windup, and mixer behavior correct, and tune the inner rate loop before the outer attitude loop. Then extend the controller according to the source of variation: use gain scheduling for measurable operating regimes, adaptive estimation or MRAC for online parameter changes, observers and feedforward for disturbances, and fuzzy, neural, or reinforcement-learning layers only when their additional complexity is justified by evidence and protected by hard bounds.

Optimal parameter selection is a constrained multiobjective problem. The strongest workflow combines plant characterization, bandwidth-separated cascaded tuning, classical or autotuned initialization, model-based or multiobjective refinement, and validation across the actual flight envelope. The available evidence supports substantial improvements from scheduling, adaptation, observers, and optimized tuning, but it does not support a universal ranking or a universal PID parameter set for all UAVs.
